title: The Sahara: World's Largest Hot Desert
summary: Why the Sahara is the world's largest hot desert, how its extreme conditions shape the land, and how people have lived there for thousands of years.
poll: No one should try to live in a place as harsh as the Sahara.

versions.title: The Biggest Hot Desert
versions.text:
The Sahara is a desert. It is a hot, dry land. It is a very big desert. It is the biggest hot desert in the world. It is in North Africa.

The Sahara is huge. Few people live there. It is hard to live in. That is why it is so quiet. Not much grows there.

Much of the land is flat rock. Some parts have deep sand. Wind blows the sand around. It piles the sand into hills. A hill of sand is a dune. Some dunes rise very high. The wind can change their shape.

The days get very hot. The sun beats down hard. The nights can turn cold. Rain almost never falls.

Some people live here too. They move from place to place. We call them nomads. A camel helps them move. It can walk far in the sand. It does not need much water.

A green spot in the desert is an oasis. Water comes up from the ground there. Palm trees can grow at an oasis. Small towns can grow there too.

versions.title: The Biggest Hot Desert
versions.text:
The Sahara is a huge desert. It is the biggest hot desert in the world. It covers a large part of the land.

The Sahara is very big. Most of it is dry, flat rock. Some parts are covered in deep sand. The wind piles this sand into tall hills. A hill of sand is called a dune. Some dunes rise higher than a house.

The days in the Sahara get very hot. The sun beats down hard. At night, the air can turn cold. Rain almost never falls here.

Some people who live here move from place to place. They are called nomads. They travel with their animals to find new land. A camel helps people travel across the sand. It can walk for many days. It needs very little water.

A green place in the desert is called an oasis. Water rises up from under the ground there. Palm trees can grow at an oasis. Small towns often grow up near the water too.

versions.title: The Sahara: The World's Biggest Hot Desert
versions.text:
The Sahara is an enormous desert in North Africa. It is the biggest hot desert in the whole world. It stretches across many countries.

Most of the Sahara is flat rock. Some parts are covered by huge seas of sand. Strong wind piles this sand into tall dunes. Some dunes rise higher than a tall building. The wind slowly changes the shape of the dunes.

Daytime in the Sahara gets very hot. It can climb past 40 degrees. At night, though, the air can turn cold. Rain almost never falls across this desert.

Some people who live here move from place to place with their animals. They are called nomads. One well-known group of nomads is the Tuareg. A camel helps people cross the desert. It can walk for days with very little water.

A green place where water reaches the surface is called an oasis. Date palms grow well at an oasis. Small towns have grown up around this water for a long time.

versions.title: The Sahara: The World's Biggest Hot Desert

The Sahara stretches across the whole top of Africa. It is the biggest hot desert in the entire world. It reaches from one ocean to another sea.

Most of the Sahara is flat, rocky land. Some parts are covered by huge seas of sand called ergs. Strong winds pile this loose sand into tall dunes. Some dunes rise higher than a tall building. The wind slowly reshapes the dunes over time.

Daytime heat in the Sahara can climb above 40 degrees Celsius. The heat can feel truly extreme. At night, though, the air can turn cold. Rain almost never falls across this vast, dry land.

Nomadic groups such as the Tuareg have lived in the Sahara for many years. They move from place to place with their herds of animals. A camel helps people cross this hard land. It can walk for days with very little water.

A green place where water from below reaches the top is called an oasis. Date palms and other plants grow there. Small towns have grown up around this water for a long time.

versions.title: The Sahara: The World's Largest Hot Desert
versions.text:
The Sahara stretches across the whole top of Africa. It is the largest hot desert region on Earth. It covers about nine million square kilometers. It reaches from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea.

Most of the Sahara is flat, rocky plateau and gravel. Some areas are covered by huge seas of sand called ergs. Strong winds pile this sand into tall dunes. Some dunes rise higher than a skyscraper. The wind keeps changing their shape.

Daytime temperatures can climb above 50 degrees Celsius. That is an extreme amount of heat. At night, the air can turn surprisingly cold. Rain almost never falls in this vast, dry region.

For centuries, traders crossed the desert in camel caravans. They followed routes between West Africa and the Mediterranean coast. They carried salt and gold. Camels earned the nickname "ships of the desert." They can travel for days with very little water.

Nomadic groups such as the Tuareg have lived in this region for generations. They move with their herds to find fresh land. Camels helped them travel far.

A green place where water reaches the surface is called an oasis. Towns have grown up around this water along the old trade routes.

versions.title: The Sahara: An Ocean of Sand and Stone
versions.text:
The Sahara stretches across the entire northern third of Africa, and it is the largest hot desert region on Earth. It covers about nine million square kilometers, nearly as large as the United States, reaching from the Atlantic Ocean in the west to the Red Sea in the east.

Most of the Sahara is flat, rocky plateau and gravel rather than sand. Some regions are covered by huge seas of sand called ergs. Powerful winds pile this sand into towering dunes, and some of the tallest rise higher than a skyscraper. Wind erosion keeps slowly reshaping their surface over time.

This is a profoundly arid region. Daytime temperatures can climb above 50 degrees Celsius, among the hottest ever recorded on the planet, while at night the dry air loses heat quickly and can turn surprisingly cold. Rain almost never falls, and the sparse vegetation here has adapted to months without water.

Indigenous communities have lived in the Sahara for thousands of years. Nomadic groups such as the Tuareg travel constantly with their herds of goats and camels, moving to find fresh grazing land before each dry season returns.

For centuries, traders crossed the desert in long camel caravans, carrying salt and gold between West Africa and the Mediterranean coast. Camels earned the nickname "ships of the desert" because they need so little water.

Scientists have found ancient rock paintings across the Sahara that show giraffes, hippos, and cattle, suggesting the region once held grasslands and lakes during a period called the Green Sahara.

In the early twentieth century, European expedition teams crossed the Sahara looking for new routes, and they depended on local guides who knew where the desert's hidden wells, or oases, could be found. Even today, people remember these expeditions as proof of how much knowledge the desert people had gathered over many generations.

Most of the Sahara consists of flat, rocky plateau and gravel rather than sand, but in certain regions enormous seas of sand known as ergs blanket the ground. Powerful winds accumulate this loose sand into towering dunes, and the tallest rise higher than a skyscraper, their forms continuously reworked through ongoing erosion as the wind perpetually reshapes the surface over long stretches of geological time.

Daytime temperatures in the Sahara can climb above 50 degrees Celsius, among the hottest readings ever recorded anywhere on the planet, while nights can turn surprisingly cold because the arid desert air loses heat rapidly once the sun sets below the horizon. Rain almost never falls across this extreme, arid region, and the sparse vegetation that manages to survive has adapted to going months, or even years, without a single drop of precipitation.

Despite these harsh conditions, indigenous communities have inhabited the Sahara for thousands of years. Nomadic groups such as the Tuareg travel with their herds of goats and camels, relocating constantly in order to locate fresh grazing land before each dry season returns in full force.

For centuries, traders crossed the desert in long camel caravans, carrying salt and gold between West Africa and the bustling cities along the Mediterranean coast. Camels earned the enduring nickname "ships of the desert" because they can travel for days through deep, shifting sand while requiring remarkably little water.

Scientists have discovered ancient rock paintings scattered across the Sahara that depict giraffes, hippos, and herds of cattle grazing beside open water. These paintings strongly suggest that thousands of years ago, during a period known as the Green Sahara, this region held grasslands and lakes rather than the endless sand and stone seen today.

In the early twentieth century, European expedition teams crossed the Sahara seeking new routes and resources, and they depended heavily on local guides whose generations of accumulated knowledge revealed the desert's hidden wells. A green place where underground water reaches the surface is called an oasis, and busy towns have formed around this precious water along the ancient trade routes across countless generations.

versions.title: The Sahara: An Ocean of Sand and Stone
versions.text:
The Sahara stretches across the entire northern third of the African continent, ranking as the largest hot desert region on Earth and one of the most extensive, inhospitable landscapes anywhere on the planet. Covering approximately nine million square kilometers, an area nearly as large as the United States, it extends from the Atlantic Ocean in the west all the way to the Red Sea in the east, encompassing a remarkable diversity of terrain within its vast boundaries.

Contrary to popular imagination, most of the Sahara consists of flat, rocky plateau and gravel rather than rolling sand, though certain regions are blanketed by enormous seas of sand known as ergs. Powerful winds accumulate this loose sand into towering dunes, some rising higher than a skyscraper, their forms continuously reshaped through persistent erosion as the wind perpetually reworks the surface across immense stretches of geological time, carving plateaus and exposing ancient bedrock in the process.

This is a profoundly arid environment, where daytime temperatures regularly climb above 50 degrees Celsius, among the hottest readings ever recorded on the planet, while nights turn surprisingly cold as the dry air loses heat with remarkable speed after sunset. Rain almost never falls, and the sparse vegetation that survives here has adapted to endure months, or even years, without a single drop of precipitation.

Remarkably, indigenous communities have inhabited this unforgiving landscape for thousands of years. Nomadic groups such as the Tuareg move constantly with their herds of goats and camels, searching for fresh grazing land before each dry season returns, relying on generations of accumulated environmental knowledge to survive conditions that would overwhelm an unprepared traveler.

For centuries, traders crossed the desert in long camel caravans, exchanging salt and gold between West Africa and the bustling cities along the Mediterranean coast, and camels earned their enduring nickname "ships of the desert" for their ability to travel for days through shifting sand while requiring remarkably little water.

Ancient rock paintings scattered across the Sahara depict giraffes, hippos, and herds of cattle grazing beside open water, striking evidence that thousands of years ago, during a period scientists call the Green Sahara, this region held expansive grasslands and lakes instead of today's endless sand and stone, a dramatic transformation driven by gradual shifts in Earth's orbit and rainfall patterns.

In the early twentieth century, European expedition teams crossed the Sahara seeking new routes and resources, depending entirely on local guides whose inherited knowledge revealed the desert's hidden wells, oases where underground water finally reaches the surface and makes settled life, and date palm cultivation, possible at all.

versions.title: The Sahara: An Ocean of Sand and Stone
versions.text:
The Sahara stretches across the entire northern third of the African continent, ranking as the largest hot desert region on Earth and constituting one of the most extensive, inhospitable landscapes found anywhere on the planet. Covering approximately nine million square kilometers, an area nearly as large as the United States, it extends from the Atlantic Ocean in the west all the way to the Red Sea in the east, encompassing a remarkable diversity of terrain within its vast and varied boundaries.

Contrary to popular imagination, the majority of the Sahara consists of flat, rocky plateau and gravel rather than rolling sand, though certain regions are blanketed by enormous seas of sand known as ergs. Powerful winds accumulate this loose sand into towering dunes, some rising higher than a skyscraper, their forms continuously reshaped through persistent erosion as the wind perpetually reworks the surface across immense stretches of geological time, carving exposed plateaus and gradually revealing ancient bedrock beneath the shifting grains.

This constitutes a profoundly arid environment, one in which daytime temperatures regularly climb above 50 degrees Celsius, among the hottest readings ever recorded anywhere on the planet, while nights turn surprisingly cold as the dry air loses accumulated heat with remarkable speed following sunset. Rain almost never falls, and the sparse vegetation that manages to survive here has adapted over countless generations to endure months, or even years, without a single drop of precipitation.

Remarkably, indigenous communities have inhabited this unforgiving landscape for thousands of years. Nomadic groups such as the Tuareg move constantly with their herds of goats and camels, perpetually searching for fresh grazing land before each dry season returns, relying on generations of accumulated environmental knowledge to survive conditions that would overwhelm any unprepared traveler attempting the crossing alone.

For centuries, traders crossed the desert in long camel caravans, exchanging salt and gold between West Africa and the bustling cities along the Mediterranean coast, and camels earned their enduring nickname "ships of the desert" for their remarkable ability to travel for days through shifting sand while requiring astonishingly little water.

Ancient rock paintings scattered across the Sahara depict giraffes, hippos, and herds of cattle grazing beside open water, striking evidence that thousands of years ago, during a period scientists call the Green Sahara, this region held expansive grasslands and lakes instead of today's endless sand and stone, a dramatic transformation driven by gradual, cyclical shifts in Earth's orbit and the rainfall patterns those shifts produced.

In the early twentieth century, European expedition teams crossed the Sahara seeking new routes and resources, depending entirely on local guides whose inherited knowledge revealed the desert's hidden wells, oases where underground water finally reaches the surface and makes settled life, extensive date palm cultivation, and centuries of continuous trade possible in a landscape that otherwise permits almost nothing to survive.

questions.stem: Why do nomadic groups like the Tuareg keep moving with their herds?
options: To find fresh grazing land before the dry season returns
To avoid meeting traders on the long roads of the desert
To search for snow in the mountains far to the north
To escape from camels that chase them each day
questions.why: The article says nomads move constantly to find fresh grazing land before each dry season returns.

wrong.B: The article does not say nomads avoid traders; caravans and nomads both cross the desert.
wrong.C: The Sahara almost never has snow.
wrong.D: Nomads travel with camels; they do not escape from them.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the article?
options: By telling a made-up story about one trader's life, from his birth to his death
By describing the desert's size and climate, then the people, trade, and history connected to it
By listing the steps to cross a desert on foot, with a note on water and food
By comparing the Sahara to a rainforest in every paragraph, from the plants to the weather
questions.why: The article first describes the Sahara's location, size, landscape, and climate, then moves on to the nomads, traders, and oases found there.

wrong.A: The article is not a story about one person.
wrong.C: The article does not give steps for crossing on foot.
wrong.D: The article never compares the Sahara to a rainforest.

MID.prompt: Explain how people have managed to live and travel in the Sahara despite its extreme conditions. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained how people live or travel in the Sahara.
I used at least two details from the article.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: People have found ways to survive the Sahara's extreme conditions for thousands of years. Nomadic groups such as the Tuareg move constantly with their herds of goats and camels to find fresh grazing land before each dry season returns. Traders also crossed the desert in long camel caravans, carrying salt and gold between West Africa and the Mediterranean coast, because camels can travel for days through sand while needing very little water.

keyWords.definition: having very little rain and extremely dry land
keyWords.example: Few crops can grow in such an arid climate without irrigation.

keyWords.definition: the gradual wearing away of rock or soil by wind or water
keyWords.example: Years of erosion carved the narrow canyon out of soft rock.

keyWords.definition: the plants growing in a particular area
keyWords.example: Thick vegetation covered the hillside after the rainy season.

keyWords.definition: originally living in a place, rather than arriving from somewhere else
keyWords.example: The museum displayed tools made by an indigenous community long ago.

keyWords.definition: a long, organized journey made for a special purpose, such as exploring
keyWords.example: The team spent a year preparing for their expedition across the ice.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: The Sahara has looked exactly the same since the planet formed, and its sand never moves or changes, even in the strongest wind.
The Sahara is a vast, arid desert whose extreme conditions have shaped its landscape, its history, and the indigenous people connected to it.
No living thing has ever been able to survive in the Sahara, not even a small plant, an insect, or a person, so the whole desert is empty and silent.
The Sahara receives more rainfall than a tropical rainforest, so its land is green and full of rivers and lakes.
questions.why: The article explains the desert's size, climate, and erosion-shaped landscape, and how indigenous nomads, ancient traders, and scientists all connect to this extreme region.

wrong.A: The rock paintings show the Green Sahara was once very different.
wrong.C: The Tuareg and other species have survived there for thousands of years.
wrong.D: The article says rain almost never falls in the Sahara.

questions.stem: Why do the tallest dunes in the Sahara keep changing shape over time?
options: Erosion from wind continually reshapes the loose sand
Rivers wash the sand downhill every year
Camels flatten the dunes as they slowly walk across them
Nomads rebuild the dunes by hand
questions.why: The wind keeps slowly reshaping the dunes over time.

wrong.B: The article does not mention rivers shaping the dunes.
wrong.C: Camels walk across the sand but do not reshape entire dunes.
wrong.D: The article does not say nomads rebuild dunes.

questions.stem: According to the article, how has the sparse vegetation of the Sahara adapted to the climate?
options: It grows only during the coldest nights
It depends entirely on nomads for water
It can survive months or years without any rain
It grows only inside ancient rock paintings
questions.why: The few plants there have adapted to going months, or even years, without rain.

wrong.A: The article links the vegetation's survival to dryness, not to nighttime cold.
wrong.B: The article does not say plants depend on nomads for water.
wrong.D: Rock paintings are art, not living plants.

questions.stem: In the article, the word indigenous describes —
options: travelers who recently arrived from Europe
communities that have inhabited a place for a very long time
animals that only live in zoos
scientists who study and carefully record ancient rock paintings
questions.why: The article describes indigenous communities, such as the Tuareg, who have inhabited the Sahara for thousands of years, long before any outside explorers arrived.

wrong.A: European expedition teams arrived much later, which is the opposite of indigenous.
wrong.C: The word does not refer to zoo animals.
wrong.D: Scientists studying the art are not what the word indigenous describes.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why did European expedition teams depend on local guides when crossing the Sahara?
options: The guides' generations of accumulated knowledge revealed the desert's hidden wells
The guides owned every oasis in the whole region and sold the water to travelers
The guides could make rain fall whenever needed by the explorers
The guides had modern maps the explorers lacked, drawn by the government
questions.why: In the article, the expedition teams depended on local guides whose generations of accumulated knowledge revealed hidden wells, essential for survival in such an arid place.

wrong.B: The article does not say guides owned the oases.
wrong.C: No one in the article can control the rain.
wrong.D: The article credits the guides' own knowledge, not modern maps.

questions.stem: In what order did these developments most likely occur?
options: European expeditions cross the Sahara, the Green Sahara existed, camel caravans begin trading salt and gold
Camel caravans begin trading salt and gold, European expeditions cross the Sahara, the Green Sahara existed
European expeditions cross the Sahara, camel caravans begin trading salt and gold, the Green Sahara existed
The Green Sahara existed, camel caravans begin trading salt and gold, European expeditions cross the Sahara
questions.why: The Green Sahara existed many thousands of years ago, the salt and gold caravan trade developed over later centuries, and European expeditions crossed the desert in the early twentieth century.

wrong.A: The Green Sahara came first, long before any expeditions.
wrong.B: The Green Sahara predates the caravan trade by thousands of years.
wrong.C: The Green Sahara came before both the trade and the expeditions.

questions.stem: What can readers infer from the rock paintings of giraffes, hippos, and cattle found in the Sahara?
options: Artists today still paint these animals in the desert for tourists
The Sahara's climate was once wet enough to support grasslands and lakes
These animals currently live throughout the whole Sahara in herds
The paintings prove the Sahara has never changed in its history
questions.why: Giraffes, hippos, and cattle all need grass and water to survive, so paintings of them suggest the Sahara once had a much wetter climate.

wrong.A: The paintings are ancient, not recent.
wrong.C: These animals do not live across today's dry Sahara.
wrong.D: The paintings are evidence of dramatic change, not changelessness.

questions.stem: Why does the author likely include the detail about the Green Sahara near the middle of the article?
options: To argue that hippos should be reintroduced to the desert today for the tourists
To show that the region's climate and landscape have changed dramatically over time
To explain exactly how rock paintings are made, using stones and animal fat
To describe what modern explorers eat during expeditions and where they sleep
questions.why: The Green Sahara detail shows that today's extremely arid desert was once a very different, much wetter landscape, highlighting dramatic environmental change.

wrong.A: The article does not suggest reintroducing hippos.
wrong.C: The article does not explain painting techniques.
wrong.D: The article does not describe expedition food.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says no one should try to live in a place as harsh as the Sahara. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the article about its climate, history, and people.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the article.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that no one should try to live in a place as harsh as the Sahara. Indigenous communities such as the Tuareg have inhabited this arid region for thousands of years, moving with their herds to find fresh grazing land before each dry season. The long history of camel caravans carrying salt and gold across the desert also shows that people built successful lives and trade routes there. Someone might argue that temperatures above 50 degrees Celsius and almost no rainfall make survival impossible, but generations of accumulated knowledge about hidden wells and oases prove that careful, well-prepared living in the Sahara has always been possible.

LOW.stem: What is much of the land in the Sahara like?
options: Soft green grass
Flat rock
Thick forest
Cold ice
LOW.why: In the text, much of the land is flat rock.

wrong.A: Not much grows in the Sahara.
wrong.C: A thick forest does not grow in the desert.
wrong.D: The Sahara is hot, not icy.

LOW.stem: In the article, the word huge means —
options: very cold
quite quiet
rather old
very big
LOW.why: The Sahara is described as a very big desert, so huge means very big.

wrong.A: The days are hot, so huge does not mean cold.
wrong.B: Quiet is a different idea in the text.
wrong.C: Age is not the idea of the sentence.

LOW.stem: Why can palm trees grow at an oasis?
options: Water comes up from the ground there.
Wind piles sand around them there.
The sun is much cooler there.
Nomads plant them each night.
LOW.why: In the text, water comes up from the ground at an oasis, so palm trees can grow there.

wrong.B: Wind piles sand into dunes, which does not help trees.
wrong.C: The text does not say the sun is cooler at an oasis.
wrong.D: The text does not say nomads plant them.

LOW.stem: Why does not much grow in the Sahara?
options: Wind blows all the plants away.
Camels eat every plant.
Rain almost never falls.
The sand is too cold.
LOW.why: Rain almost never falls in the Sahara, so there is little water for plants.

wrong.A: The text says wind moves sand, not plants.
wrong.B: Camels eating every plant is not stated.
wrong.D: The days are hot, not the sand cold.

MID.stem: Between which two bodies of water does the Sahara reach?
options: The Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea
The Red Sea to the Arctic Ocean
The Pacific Ocean to the Red Sea
The Indian Ocean to the Atlantic
MID.why: The text says the Sahara reaches from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea.

wrong.B: The Arctic Ocean is not mentioned.
wrong.C: The Pacific Ocean is not mentioned.
wrong.D: The Indian Ocean is not mentioned.

MID.stem: In the article, the word extreme most nearly means —
options: very small
quite pleasant
very great
slightly cool
MID.why: Temperatures above 50 degrees are called an extreme amount of heat, meaning a very great amount.

wrong.A: Small does not fit a very high heat.
wrong.B: Heat above 50 degrees is not pleasant.
wrong.D: The sentence is about strong heat.

MID.stem: What shapes the sand into tall dunes?
options: Rain falling all year
Camel caravans crossing
Rivers of water
Strong winds
MID.why: The text says strong winds pile sand into tall dunes.

wrong.A: Rain almost never falls in the Sahara.
wrong.B: Caravans are traders, not a force that makes dunes.
wrong.C: The Sahara is a dry region.

MID.stem: Why did towns grow up around oases along old trade routes?
options: Traders had no need for water
Travelers needed the water there
Oases were far from the routes
Towns are always built in sand
MID.why: An oasis is where water reaches the surface, and people crossing the desert needed that water.

wrong.A: Traders in a dry desert needed water.
wrong.C: The towns grew along the old trade routes.
wrong.D: In the text, towns grew where there was water.

HIGH.stem: Which country is the Sahara's size compared to?
options: The country of Egypt
The country of Spain
The United States
The country of Japan
HIGH.why: The text says the Sahara is nearly as large as the United States.

wrong.A: Egypt is not used for the comparison.
wrong.B: Spain is not used for the comparison.
wrong.D: Japan is not used for the comparison.

HIGH.stem: In the article, the word arid most nearly means —
options: very dry
very windy
very rocky
very cold
HIGH.why: The Sahara is called arid because rain almost never falls there, so arid means very dry.

wrong.B: The text describes wind elsewhere, not as arid.
wrong.C: Rocky describes the land, not the word arid.
wrong.D: The days are very hot.

HIGH.stem: Why can the Sahara turn cold at night?
options: Rain falls every evening.
The sand holds heat all night.
Strong winds blow in from the sea.
The dry air loses heat quickly.
HIGH.why: In the text, at night the dry air loses heat quickly and can turn surprisingly cold.

wrong.A: Rain almost never falls.
wrong.B: The sand losing heat is the reverse of holding it.
wrong.C: Winds from the sea are not mentioned.

HIGH.stem: What does before each dry season returns suggest about the Tuareg's travels?
options: They stay in one place all year
They follow a pattern each year
They only travel in the dark
They stop moving in winter
HIGH.why: If dry seasons return and the Tuareg move before each one, their travel follows a yearly pattern.

wrong.A: The text says they travel constantly.
wrong.C: Nothing is said about traveling in the dark.
wrong.D: Winter is not mentioned.
